title: PKI
text:
Public keys and private keys. A key pair is two related keys. What one does, only the other can undo: data encrypted to the public key needs the private key to decrypt, and a signature made with the private key verifies with the public key. The private key never needs to leave its owner.
What a certificate does and does not prove. A certificate is a signed statement from a certificate authority (CA): this public key belongs to this name, for these uses, during this time. It does not prove the site is safe, that the operator is who you assume, or that the private key has not been stolen since.
Certificate authorities and trust. You trust a CA because a trust store says to: the operating system’s, the browser’s, or one you configured. A certificate is only as trustworthy as the CA that signed it and the store that trusts that CA.

The profile for certificates on the internet is RFC 5280.

PowerShell and .NET
.NET reads certificate files directly. This function returns the fields you usually want, including the names in the SAN:
function Get-CertificateInfo {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Shows the main fields of a certificate file (PEM or DER), including the DNS names in its SAN.
    .EXAMPLE
        Get-CertificateInfo -Path .\training-leaf.pem
    .EXAMPLE
        Get-ChildItem *.pem, *.cer | Get-CertificateInfo
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        # The certificate file; also accepts files piped from Get-ChildItem
        [Parameter(Mandatory, ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName)]
        [Alias('FullName')]
        [string]$Path
    )

    process {
        # .NET needs a full path, so resolve relative paths like .\leaf.pem first
        $FullPath = (Resolve-Path -Path $Path).ProviderPath
        $Cert = [System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates.X509Certificate2]::new($FullPath)

        # The SAN extension (OID 2.5.29.17) formats as "DNS Name=a.example, DNS Name=b.example"
        $San = $Cert.Extensions | Where-Object { $_.Oid.Value -eq '2.5.29.17' }
        $DnsNames = if ($San) {
            $San.Format($false) -split ',\s*' |
                Where-Object { $_ -like 'DNS Name=*' } |
                ForEach-Object { $_ -replace '^DNS Name=', '' }
        }

        [pscustomobject]@{
            Subject      = $Cert.Subject
            Issuer       = $Cert.Issuer
            NotBefore    = $Cert.NotBefore
            NotAfter     = $Cert.NotAfter
            DnsNames     = $DnsNames
            Thumbprint   = $Cert.Thumbprint
            SerialNumber = $Cert.SerialNumber
        }
    }
}

title: PKI
text:
Certificate formats

ASN.1 describes the structure. DER is the binary encoding of that structure.
PEM is Base64 DER between -----BEGIN ...----- and -----END ...----- lines (RFC 7468). The label says what is inside: CERTIFICATE, CERTIFICATE REQUEST, PRIVATE KEY, PKCS7.
A file extension does not necessarily tell you what’s inside.




Extension
Usually holds
Contains a private key?




.cer, .crt
One certificate, DER or PEM
No


.pem
Anything PEM: certificates, chains, keys, CSRs
Possibly; look at the labels


.key
A private key, usually PEM
Yes


.p7b, .p7c
PKCS #7 / CMS bundle of certificates (RFC 5652)
No


.pfx, .p12
PKCS #12 archive: certificate, chain and private key, password protected (RFC 7292)
Usually yes


.csr, .req
PKCS #10 certificate request
No



Same certificate, two encodings. training-leaf.pem and training-leaf.der are the same certificate. Their certificate fingerprints match:
sha256 Fingerprint=56:6D:45:25:0C:E6:AA:7F:F4:C7:DB:55:76:B8:1E:B8:B6:57:C2:C6:06:7D:5F:AA:81:2D:39:5B:EE:69:AE:67
The SHA-256 file hash of the DER file is the same value, because a certificate fingerprint is the hash of its DER encoding. The PEM file’s hash differs, because it is text.

Converting
openssl x509 -in training-leaf.der -inform der -out leaf.pem          # DER to PEM
openssl x509 -in training-leaf.pem -outform der -out leaf.der         # PEM to DER
openssl pkcs7 -in bundle.p7b -print_certs -out bundle.pem             # PKCS #7 to PEM certificates
openssl pkcs12 -in server.pfx -nokeys -out server-certs.pem           # certificates out of a PFX
certutil -encode training-leaf.der leaf.pem     # DER to PEM (Base64)
certutil -decode training-leaf.pem leaf.der     # PEM to DER

title: PKI
text:
Certificate requests and issuance

Certificate signing requests (PKCS #10)
A CSR (RFC 2986) carries the public key, the requested subject and requested extensions, signed with the matching private key. The signature proves the requester holds the private key; it proves nothing about whether they should get the name. That is the CA’s job.
openssl req -in training-request.csr -noout -text -verify
Certificate request self-signature verify OK
Certificate Request:
    Data:
        Version: 1 (0x0)
        Subject: C=US, ST=Wisconsin, L=Curdsville, O=Squeaky Curds Co-op, CN=squeakycurds.example
        ...
        Attributes:
            Requested Extensions:
                X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
                    DNS:squeakycurds.example
The CSR and the issued certificate carry the same public key:
openssl req  -in training-request.csr -noout -pubkey | openssl sha256
openssl x509 -in training-leaf.pem    -noout -pubkey | openssl sha256
# both: 7a764e059181f774138b29119eab1ab71dce68e5829aba787c3a7f3fb9deecb0
Creating a key pair and request with OpenSSL (the key stays with you):
openssl req -new -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout server.key -out server.csr \
    -subj "/CN=squeakycurds.example" -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:squeakycurds.example"


Internal CAs: AD CS and certificate templates
Active Directory Certificate Services issues against certificate templates, which set key usage, EKU, validity, who may enroll and whether the subject comes from the request or from AD. Request with certreq and an INF file:
[NewRequest]
Subject = "CN=squeakycurds.example"
KeyAlgorithm = RSA
KeyLength = 2048
Exportable = FALSE
MachineKeySet = TRUE
RequestType = PKCS10

[Extensions]
2.5.29.17 = "{text}"
_continue_ = "dns=squeakycurds.example&"

[RequestAttributes]
CertificateTemplate = WebServer
certreq -new request.inf request.csr        # create the key pair and request
certreq -submit -config "CA01\Contoso Issuing CA" request.csr server.cer
certreq -accept server.cer                  # install, pairing with the pending private key
Replace CA01\Contoso Issuing CA with your CAHost\CA name. The CertificateTemplate line needs a domain-joined machine that can see the template; without one, certreq -new reports “Template not found.” To make a request without AD CS, remove that line and set MachineKeySet = FALSE.
Template settings that let the requester supply the subject name, combined with a client authentication EKU and broad enrollment rights, are a well-known AD CS privilege escalation path (“ESC1” in SpecterOps’ Certified Pre-Owned). Review who can enroll in such templates.


ACME and automated issuance
ACME (RFC 8555) automates the whole cycle: create an account, place an order for names, prove control of each name, send a CSR, download the certificate, renew before expiry. Proof of control is a challenge:



Challenge
How control is proven
Notes




http-01
Serve a token at http://<name>/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token> on port 80
No wildcards


dns-01
Publish a TXT record at _acme-challenge.<name>
Works for wildcards and internal-only hosts with public DNS


tls-alpn-01
Present a special certificate on port 443 (RFC 8737)
No wildcards



The CA checks control of the name, then issues; it does not check who you are. That is domain validation.

title: PKI
text:
Putting a certificate to use
A service needs three things:

The certificate.
The private key that matches it.
The intermediate certificates between it and a root clients trust.

The certificate presented by a service is separate from the trust configured on a client. The server sends its leaf and intermediates; the client supplies the root from its own store. A server that omits its intermediate can work in one browser, which has the intermediate cached or fetches it from the AIA URL, and fail in another client, such as a script, an appliance or a mail server, that does neither.
On Windows the private key lives with the certificate in the store (or in a .pfx). On Linux it is usually a separate PEM file. Check that a certificate and key match by comparing public keys:
openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -pubkey | openssl sha256
openssl pkey -in server.key -pubout | openssl sha256

title: PKI
text:
Certificate validation
RFC 5280 §6 defines path validation; RFC 9525 defines name matching for TLS. A client checks:








Check
Question
Fails when




Name
Does a SAN entry match the name I asked for?
Wrong host, missing SAN, CN-only certificate


Dates
Is now between Not Before and Not After, for every certificate in the chain?
Expired, not yet valid, wrong clock


Chain
Can I build a path to a certificate in my trust store, with valid signatures?
Missing intermediate, untrusted or private root


Constraints
Is every issuer a CA, within its path length?
CA:FALSE certificate used as an issuer


Usage
Do key usage and EKU permit this purpose?
Server certificate used for client authentication


Revocation
Has the CA revoked anything in the chain?
Revoked; or, depending on client, status unavailable




Validation failures, reproduced
Each of these was run against the sample files with OpenSSL 3.5.
Untrusted root (the root is not in any trust store):
$ openssl verify training-leaf.pem
C=US, ST=Wisconsin, L=Curdsville, O=Squeaky Curds Co-op, CN=squeakycurds.example
error 20 at 0 depth lookup: unable to get local issuer certificate
error training-leaf.pem: verification failed
Supplying the root as a trust anchor makes it pass: openssl verify -CAfile training-root.pem training-leaf.pem returns training-leaf.pem: OK.
Incorrect name:
$ openssl verify -CAfile training-root.pem -verify_hostname www.squeakycurds.example training-leaf.pem
C=US, ST=Wisconsin, L=Curdsville, O=Squeaky Curds Co-op, CN=squeakycurds.example
error 62 at 0 depth lookup: hostname mismatch
error training-leaf.pem: verification failed
squeakycurds.example passes; www.squeakycurds.example does not, because the SAN lists only squeakycurds.example. A wildcard *.squeakycurds.example would match www.squeakycurds.example but not squeakycurds.example or a.b.squeakycurds.example (RFC 9525 §6.3).
Expired (checking as of December 1, 2027):
$ openssl verify -CAfile training-root.pem -attime 1827619200 training-leaf.pem
C=US, ST=Wisconsin, L=Curdsville, O=Squeaky Curds Co-op, CN=squeakycurds.example
error 10 at 0 depth lookup: certificate has expired
error training-leaf.pem: verification failed
Checking as of September 1, 2026 reports error 9 at 1 depth lookup: certificate is not yet valid: depth 1 is the root, which was not yet valid either.
Wrong usage (the leaf’s EKU is server authentication only):
$ openssl verify -CAfile training-root.pem -purpose sslclient training-leaf.pem
C=US, ST=Wisconsin, L=Curdsville, O=Squeaky Curds Co-op, CN=squeakycurds.example
error 26 at 0 depth lookup: unsuitable certificate purpose
error training-leaf.pem: verification failed
Windows view of the untrusted root. certutil -verify training-leaf.pem on a machine without the training root:
A certificate chain could not be built to a trusted root authority. 0x800b010a (-2146762486 CERT_E_CHAINING)
------------------------------------
Incomplete certificate chain
Cannot find certificate:
    CN=Squeaky Curd Root CA, O=Cheese Curd Authority, S=Wisconsin, C=US
Cert is an End Entity certificate

ERROR: Verifying leaf certificate revocation status returned The revocation function was unable to check revocation because the revocation server was offline. 0x80092013 (-2146885613 CRYPT_E_REVOCATION_OFFLINE)
CertUtil: The revocation function was unable to check revocation because the revocation server was offline.

CertUtil: -verify command completed successfully.
Note the last line: certutil reports the command completed, not that the certificate is valid. Read the errors above it. certutil -verify -urlfetch also retrieves AIA and CRL URLs and reports each one, which is the quickest way to find a broken CRL distribution point on an internal CA.


Revocation: CRLs and OCSP

CRL (Certificate Revocation List): a signed list of revoked serial numbers the CA publishes at the URL in the CRL Distribution Points extension. Clients download and cache it.
OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol): ask the CA’s responder about one certificate. Responses can be stapled by the server so the client does not have to ask.

Client behavior varies, and is the part people get wrong:

Browsers mostly do not check online. Chrome relies on CRLSets, a curated list pushed with updates, rather than fetching CRLs or OCSP for most certificates. Other browsers have their own approaches, so test the client you care about.
Public CAs are moving away from OCSP. Let’s Encrypt ended its OCSP service on August 6, 2025 and now publishes revocation only through CRLs (announcement).
Windows (CryptoAPI) checks CRLs and OCSP and caches results. Whether “revocation server offline” is fatal depends on the application: some fail closed, many fail open.
Internal CAs most often break here: an expired CRL or an unreachable CDP URL causes failures in clients that do enforce revocation, such as smart card logon on domain controllers and some VPNs.

title: PKI
text:
Renewal and maintenance
Expiration is the most common certificate incident, and public certificate lifetimes are getting shorter. The CA/Browser Forum’s Baseline Requirements (§1.2.2, from ballot SC-081v3, passed April 2025) set the maximum validity of publicly trusted TLS certificates:



Issued on or after
Maximum validity




March 15, 2026
200 days


March 15, 2027
100 days


March 15, 2029
47 days



Source: CA/Browser Forum TLS Baseline Requirements. These limits do not apply to private internal CAs, which set their own policy.
What renewal involves, and what tends to be missed:

An inventory. Know which certificates exist, where they are deployed, and when they expire. For Windows, Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My -ExpiringInDays 30 on each server; for anything listening on TLS, scan it.
Replacing, not just renewing. A renewed certificate must be installed and bound everywhere the old one was: load balancers, IIS bindings, RDP, LDAPS, appliances, and anything that pinned the old one.
The new chain. A renewal can come from a different intermediate. Deploy the chain the CA gives you with the new certificate.
Automation. At 47 days, renewing by hand stops being realistic. ACME clients, AD CS autoenrollment and vendor integrations do the work; monitoring confirms it happened.

title: Building a Windows DFIR box
text:
Disposable/nonpersistent virtual machine

Return the machine to a known state.
Keep case data and analysis output separate from what gets reset.

Why disposable. Analysis tools open hostile files. Each case starts from the same known-good image, nothing carries over from the previous client, and “what version of the tool did we use” has one answer.

VMware Workstation Pro
Workstation Pro has been free for commercial, educational and personal use since November 2024 (Broadcom); download it from the Broadcom support portal.









Lives where
On reset




Windows, settings, installed tools
System disk, independent non-persistent
Discarded at power-off


Temporary files, caches, tool state
System disk
Discarded at power-off


Evidence
Host folder, shared read-only
Kept; the VM cannot change it


Analysis output, tool logs, notes
Host folder, shared read-write
Kept



Non-persistent system disk. Build the VM with a normal disk, install and configure everything, shut it down, then in VM Settings → Hard Disk → Advanced set the disk to Independent and Nonpersistent. From then on, changes are discarded when you power off the VM or restore a snapshot, and the disk is in the same state every time it starts (VMware Workstation Pro documentation). A restart inside Windows is not a power-off; shut down, and power the VM off. To update the image, switch the disk back to persistent, update, and switch it back.
Shared Folders. In VM Settings → Options → Shared Folders, add two host folders: Evidence with the Read-only attribute, so the VM can view and copy files but cannot add, change or remove them, and Cases read-write for output. With VMware Tools installed, they appear in Windows at \\vmware-host\Shared Folders\. Host file permissions still apply.
Verify it. Write a test file to Cases, try (and fail) to write one to Evidence, power off, power on, and confirm the Cases file is still there and a file you left on the desktop is gone.

title: Building a Windows DFIR box
text:
Automating the build

Decide on the Windows image and tool list.
Make setup repeatable rather than configuring it by hand each time.


Windows Server 2025
Use the Desktop Experience installation option; the analysis tools need a desktop. Microsoft’s Evaluation Center has a 180-day evaluation, which must be activated online within its first 10 days or it shuts down; activate it during the build, while the VM has a network. A licensed image is the alternative. Why Server rather than Windows 11:

Stable. Long-Term Servicing Channel: no feature updates rearranging the system between cases.
Defender is a feature. On Windows Server, Microsoft Defender Antivirus is installed as a Windows feature, Windows-Defender, so it can be removed cleanly instead of fought with (Microsoft Learn).
No TPM requirement. Microsoft lists a TPM as “required only for certain features,” such as BitLocker (hardware requirements), so the VM needs no virtual TPM, and no encryption of the VM that a virtual TPM brings with it in Workstation.



Unattended install
An unattend file (autounattend.xml) answers every question Windows Setup asks and can apply settings and run scripts. Build one with Christoph Schneegans’ unattend generator. Settings to choose for this box:



Generator setting
Why




A local administrator account
No Microsoft account; one known login


Disable User Account Control (UAC)
See UAC below


Enable long paths
Deep paths inside collections otherwise fail


Always show file extensions; show all files
invoice.pdf.exe and hidden files are visible


Do not update Last Access Time stamp
Reading a file on the box does not change its last access time


Set your time zone explicitly: (UTC) Coordinated Universal Time
See Clock below


Disable SmartScreen
Tools downloaded during the build are not blocked


Remove bloatware
Fewer distractions and background updates


FirstLogon scripts
Install Chocolatey and the tools (below)



The generator is written for Windows 10 and 11, and its files work for Windows Server 2025 once you make two choices by hand:

Product key. Choose Enter another product key and enter your own key, or the generic key for the edition from Microsoft’s KMS client product keys (Windows Server 2025 Standard: TVRH6-WHNXV-R9WG3-9XRFY-MY832). The generic key picks the edition; it does not activate Windows.
Image. Choose Select image with this name or Select image with this index, and pick a Desktop Experience image. To list the images on the ISO, mount it and run Get-WindowsImage -ImagePath D:\sources\install.wim in an elevated PowerShell (D: being the mounted ISO).

Generate the file again when you change the build, rather than editing the XML by hand.

Using the file
Windows Setup looks for a file named Autounattend.xml at the root of removable media, including read-only media such as a DVD or a mounted ISO (Windows Setup Automation Overview). The generator’s download already has that name. There are two ways to give it to Setup in a VM:

A second, small ISO that holds only autounattend.xml, attached as a second CD/DVD drive. The Windows ISO stays untouched, and you can swap answer files without rebuilding anything.
A customized Windows ISO with autounattend.xml added at its root. One ISO to attach, and it works the same on a physical machine.

Both need oscdimg.exe, which comes with the Windows ADK (install only the Deployment Tools feature).
# Where the ADK installs oscdimg
$Oscdimg = 'C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Assessment and Deployment Kit\Deployment Tools\amd64\Oscdimg\oscdimg.exe'

# A folder holding only the answer file, made into a small ISO
New-Item -Path C:\Build\Answer -ItemType Directory -Force
Copy-Item -Path "$HOME\Downloads\autounattend.xml" -Destination C:\Build\Answer
& $Oscdimg -u2 -udfver102 C:\Build\Answer C:\Build\autounattend.iso


Customizing the Windows ISO
Copy the contents of the Windows ISO to a folder, add the answer file at its root, and build a new bootable ISO. efisys_noprompt.bin is the UEFI boot file that skips “Press any key to boot from CD or DVD,” so the install runs with no one at the keyboard; use efisys.bin to keep the prompt. Images over 4.5 GB need a boot order file that puts the boot files first (Oscdimg command-line options); the script writes one from the boot and efi folders.
# Paths without spaces: oscdimg's -bootdata and -yo options do not accept them
$IsoPath = 'C:\Build\Server2025.iso'
$Build = 'C:\Build\Server2025'

# Copy everything off the Windows ISO
$Drive = (Mount-DiskImage -ImagePath $IsoPath -PassThru | Get-Volume).DriveLetter
New-Item -Path $Build -ItemType Directory -Force
Copy-Item -Path "${Drive}:\*" -Destination $Build -Recurse
Dismount-DiskImage -ImagePath $IsoPath

# Add the answer file at the root
Copy-Item -Path "$HOME\Downloads\autounattend.xml" -Destination $Build

# Boot order file: the boot files, then boot.wim, as paths relative to the root
$Order = 'C:\Build\BootOrder.txt'
Get-ChildItem -Path "$Build\boot", "$Build\efi" -Recurse -File |
    ForEach-Object { $_.FullName.Substring($Build.Length + 1) } |
    Set-Content -Path $Order -Encoding Ascii
Add-Content -Path $Order -Value 'sources\boot.wim' -Encoding Ascii

# A new ISO that boots on BIOS and UEFI
$BootData = "2#p0,e,b$Build\boot\etfsboot.com#pEF,e,b$Build\efi\microsoft\boot\efisys_noprompt.bin"
& $Oscdimg -m -o -u2 -udfver102 "-bootdata:$BootData" "-yo$Order" $Build C:\Build\Server2025-unattend.iso


Installing

In Workstation, create the VM with I will install the operating system later, so VMware’s Easy Install does not supply its own answers. Keep the default UEFI firmware.
Attach the Windows ISO and the answer-file ISO (or only the customized ISO).
Power on. With the generator’s disk and account settings, Setup partitions the disk, installs and signs in without asking anything; the FirstLogon scripts run at the first sign-in.
Check the result, then remove the ISOs from the VM.

Setup caches the answer file in C:\Windows\Panther, with the administrator password and product key in it. Delete it before you make the disk non-persistent, so it is not part of every case:
Get-ChildItem -Path C:\Windows\Panther -Filter *unattend*.xml | Remove-Item

text:
Configuring Windows for analysis

Tools that need to run as administrator.
UAC: normally I don’t disable security features, but this is a disposable VM and reducing friction matters.
Other Windows security settings as decisions specific to this machine, not general recommendations.

These are the settings, and the command for each if you apply it after setup instead of in the unattend file. Run them in an elevated PowerShell.







Setting
Command




UAC off
Set-ItemProperty -Path HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System -Name EnableLUA -Value 0, then restart


Remove Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Uninstall-WindowsFeature -Name Windows-Defender, then restart (check the name with Get-WindowsFeature *defender*)


Long paths
Set-ItemProperty -Path HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\FileSystem -Name LongPathsEnabled -Value 1


Show file extensions
Set-ItemProperty -Path HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Advanced -Name HideFileExt -Value 0


Show hidden files
Same key: Hidden = 1


Show protected system files
Same key: ShowSuperHidden = 1


No last-access updates
fsutil behavior set disablelastaccess 1


Server Manager not at every logon
Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName ServerManager \| Disable-ScheduledTask




UAC
With EnableLUA = 0, Admin Approval Mode is off and administrators run everything elevated, so tools that need administrator rights simply work. The middle ground is ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin = 0: UAC stays on and elevates without prompting, but programs still start unelevated unless asked. See Microsoft’s User Account Control settings and configuration.


Clock
Analysis output is easier to read when the screen agrees with it. NTFS stores file times in UTC (File Times), and many forensic tools, including Eric Zimmerman’s tools and Plaso, report UTC, while Windows (Explorer, Event Viewer) shows times in the system’s time zone. Either:

Use UTC as the system time zone. Everything on screen is UTC. In the unattend generator, set the time zone explicitly to (UTC) Coordinated Universal Time, or run Set-TimeZone -Id 'UTC' (Set-TimeZone).
Keep local time and add a second clock set to UTC. Control Panel → Date and Time → Additional Clocks: tick Show this clock, choose (UTC) Coordinated Universal Time and name it UTC. Hovering over the taskbar clock shows both.



Network and updates
Analysis rarely needs the internet; installs and tool updates do. Connect the VM during the build, then keep it off the internet during cases: a host-only network, or none. Hostile files cannot reach out, and the tools stay at the versions in the image. Windows Update in the middle of a case changes the system under the analysis; update the clean image on a schedule instead.

text:
Tools for analysis

Select the tools and versions.
KAPE modules for processing already-collected artifacts.


Chocolatey and Scoop
Chocolatey installs most of the list from one command, which makes the FirstLogon step one line. Its community packages are maintained by volunteers, separately from the tools’ authors: check the package page links to the real project before adding it. Scoop is an alternative that installs per user without administrator rights; it has fewer DFIR tools.
choco install -y 7zip sysinternals pwsh vscode git python wireshark cyberchef exiftool arsenalimagemounter ericzimmermantools volatility3 autopsy

# Python tools, in a new window so python and pip are on the PATH
pip install -U oletools[full]
There is no need to pin versions. The non-persistent disk keeps every tool at the version in the image until you deliberately update it, and Scoop keeps earlier versions side by side when it updates an app (scoop cleanup removes them). Record what is installed for the case notes:
choco list | Out-File -FilePath "\\vmware-host\Shared Folders\Cases\2026-0142\Notes\Tools.txt"


The tool list
The common Windows tools from DFIR distributions such as FLARE-VM and the SIFT Workstation, grouped by job.



Tool
For
Install

choco install ericzimmermantools, or his Get-ZimmermanTools.ps1

Download from Exterro

Mounting images as complete disks, so any Windows tool can read them; Free Mode includes temporary write support kept in separate differencing files

choco install autopsy

Decoding, decompressing and converting data; a local copy that works offline
choco install cyberchef


ExifTool

pestudio
First look at a Windows executable
Download from Winitor (Chocolatey flags its package as possibly broken)


oletools

pip install -U oletools[full]


Wireshark
Packet captures
choco install wireshark


Basics




7-Zip, Sysinternals, PowerShell 7, Git, Python
Archives, process and file utilities, scripting
In the choco line above


VS Code
Reading scripts, logs, JSON and CSV; editing notes
choco install vscode


Microsoft Office
Documents, and Excel for the CSVs
If your license covers it



Also common in those distributions, if your work calls for them: Notepad++ (notepadplusplus), HxD (hxd), DB Browser for SQLite (sqlitebrowser) and YARA (yara) from Chocolatey; RegRipper, capa and FLOSS from their GitHub releases (their Chocolatey packages are years behind).
Record the version of every tool used for a case in the case notes.


WSL
The Windows Subsystem for Linux runs Linux command-line tools, such as Plaso, next to the Windows tools, on the same files. Windows Server 2025 installs it with wsl.exe --install (Microsoft Learn).
Inside VMware Workstation, use WSL 1. WSL 2 runs Linux in a lightweight virtual machine, so inside this VM it needs nested virtualization: VM Settings → Processors → Virtualize Intel VT-x/EPT or AMD-V/RVI. Workstation cannot provide that while the host itself runs Hyper-V or virtualization-based security, which Memory Integrity, Credential Guard, WSL 2 and Docker Desktop on the host all turn on (Broadcom KB 389469). On a Windows 11 host with virtualization-based security running, Workstation 25.0.1 refused to power on a VM with that option set: “Virtualized Intel VT-x/EPT is not supported on this platform.” WSL 1 does not use virtualization, so it works whatever the host runs.
# WSL with the WSL 1 component, and no distribution yet; restart afterwards
wsl.exe --install --enable-wsl1 --no-distribution

# After the restart: new distributions use WSL 1, then install Ubuntu
wsl.exe --set-default-version 1
wsl.exe --install --distribution Ubuntu

# The VERSION column should show 1
wsl.exe --list --verbose
Install the distribution and its tools during the build, like everything else on the system disk. Windows drives appear in Linux under /mnt/c and so on (WSL commands).


Processing an existing artifact set with KAPE modules
KAPE has two halves: targets collect files from a system, and modules run programs against files already collected. For this box only modules apply. Modules are defined in .mkape files; the community set is maintained in KapeFiles, which includes the compound module !EZParser (runs Eric Zimmerman’s parsers over a collection).
# Module source is a collection that already exists; output goes to case storage.
.\kape.exe --msource "\\vmware-host\Shared Folders\Evidence\2026-0142\C" --mdest "\\vmware-host\Shared Folders\Cases\2026-0142\Output\EZParser" --module !EZParser
Check the switches against kape.exe --help and the KAPE documentation for the version you install.
Licensing. KAPE is free for CRT members. Commercial use, such as paid engagements, requires an enterprise license from Kroll: KAPE license agreement.

title: Building a Windows DFIR box
text:
Using and resetting the box

Run tools against existing artifacts.
Retain the results and relevant logs.
Verify the environment and reset it for the next case.

A per-case checklist:

Power on from the non-persistent image. Confirm \\vmware-host\Shared Folders\Evidence is read-only and Cases is writable.
Create the case folders with New-CaseFolder from the PowerShell page, and put the evidence in the host’s Evidence folder. Hash it on arrival with Get-FileInventory.

title: Email security
text:
Each hop adds a Received header. One server can perform several roles.


The roles come from RFC 5598, Internet Mail Architecture:








Role
What it does
Typical protocol and port




MUA, Mail User Agent
The author’s or recipient’s client: Outlook, a phone, a web client
Submission out, IMAP/POP/HTTPS in


MSA, Mail Submission Agent
Accepts new mail from users and applications, usually after they authenticate
SMTP submission: 587 (STARTTLS), 465 (implicit TLS), and sometimes 25


MTA, Mail Transfer Agent
Relays between servers; the receiving one is the MX
SMTP, port 25


MDA, Mail Delivery Agent
Puts the message in the mailbox
Local



An MSA does not have to require authentication, or use port 587. RFC 6409 §4.3 says an MSA must reject unauthenticated mail by default “unless it has already independently established authentication or authorization (such as being within a protected subnetwork)”, and §3.1 says “A site MAY choose to use port 25 for message submission.” That is how printers, scanners and line-of-business applications send: an unauthenticated relay on port 25 that trusts their IP addresses, such as an Exchange receive connector or a Microsoft 365 connector. It is also why an internal relay that accepts anything from the network is worth finding during an incident. Port 465 with TLS from the first byte is RFC 8314.
A sending MTA finds where to deliver by looking up the recipient domain’s MX records in DNS, then connects to port 25 on the lowest-preference host that answers. In Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, one service performs every role; the distinctions still show up in the headers.

title: Email security
text:
The envelope versus the message
SMTP (RFC 5321) carries a message (RFC 5322) the way an envelope carries a letter. They have separate addresses, and they do not have to agree.
In the transcripts on this page, what the client sends and what the server answers are colored differently, and annotations are gray.
S: 220 mx1.example.net ESMTP
C: EHLO out-12.esp.example
S: 250-mx1.example.net
C: MAIL FROM:<bounce-7731@mailer.esp.example>      <- envelope sender (RFC5321.MailFrom)
S: 250 2.1.0 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<pat@example.net>                         <- envelope recipient
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: DATA
S: 354 End data with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>
C: From: "Example County IT" <it-alerts@example.org>   <- message author (RFC5322.From)
C: To: pat@example.net
C: Subject: Scheduled maintenance this weekend
C:
C: ...
C: .
S: 250 2.0.0 Ok: queued

Constructed transcript with reserved example names. Each client command gets a numbered reply from the server before the next one. The two From addresses are different on purpose: this is how every email service provider and mailing list works.


MAIL FROM and RCPT TO are SMTP commands, not message headers. RCPT TO is why Bcc works: the recipient is on the envelope, not in the message.
From is the author. It is what the user sees, and it is what DMARC protects.
Sender names who actually sent the message on the author’s behalf, when that differs (RFC 5322 §3.6.2). Outlook shows it as “Sender on behalf of From”.
Return-Path is added by the final delivering server, recording the MAIL FROM address (RFC 5321 §4.4). Bounces go there.
Reply-To is where replies go. A mismatched Reply-To is common in business email compromise.

title: Email security
text:
Reading email headers
Download the constructed sample message to follow along. It uses reserved names (RFC 2606) and documentation addresses (RFC 5737).
Use Microsoft’s Message Header Analyzer. Paste headers into the web version, or install the Outlook add-in, and it lays out the hops with the delay at each one, the authentication results, and the anti-spam headers Microsoft 365 adds. The add-in needs mailbox permissions, so an administrator usually deploys it. Reading the raw headers yourself, as below, is still worth practicing: it is what you do when a tool’s interpretation looks wrong.
Return-Path: <bounce-7731@mailer.esp.example>
Received: from mx1.example.net (mx1.example.net [198.51.100.25])
    by mbox1.example.net (Postfix) with ESMTPS id 4F2A11C0042
    for <pat@example.net>; Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:02:11 -0500 (CDT)
Authentication-Results: mx1.example.net;
    spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=mailer.esp.example;
    dkim=pass header.d=example.org header.s=esp2026 header.b=Qx3fK9aL;
    dmarc=pass header.from=example.org
Received: from out-12.esp.example (out-12.esp.example [203.0.113.40])
    by mx1.example.net (Postfix) with ESMTPS id 9C77E2A0011
    for <pat@example.net>; Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:02:10 -0500 (CDT)
Authentication-Results: out-12.esp.example; dkim=pass header.d=example.org; dmarc=pass
DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; c=relaxed/relaxed; d=example.org;
    s=esp2026; t=1792177329; h=from:to:subject:date:message-id;
    bh=47DEQpj8HBSa+/TImW+5JCeuQeRkm5NMpJWZG3hSuFU=;
    b=Qx3fK9aL...
Received: from app01.example.org (app01.example.org [192.0.2.17])
    by out-12.esp.example (Postfix) with ESMTPSA id 0B1D4400A3
    for <pat@example.net>; Fri, 16 Oct 2026 19:02:09 +0000 (UTC)
From: "Example County IT" <it-alerts@example.org>
Reply-To: helpdesk@example.org
To: pat@example.net
Subject: Scheduled maintenance this weekend
Date: Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:02:08 -0500
Message-ID: <20261016190208.12345@app01.example.org>

Received headers and the path a message took
Each server prepends a Received header, so the newest is at the top. Read from the bottom up:

app01.example.org [192.0.2.17] submitted to the provider out-12.esp.example with ESMTPSA: SMTP with TLS (S) and authentication (A).
out-12.esp.example [203.0.113.40] relayed to the recipient’s MX, mx1.example.net. This is the connection SPF evaluated: 203.0.113.40 is the IP the receiver saw.
mx1.example.net handed it to the mailbox server.

Compare timestamps across hops (converting time zones) to find delays. The from name in a Received header is what the connecting host claimed in EHLO; the name and IP in parentheses are what the receiving server observed.


Authentication-Results and which system added them
RFC 8601 defines Authentication-Results. The first token is the authserv-id: the system that did the checking. This message has two. Only mx1.example.net is the recipient’s own boundary; the one from out-12.esp.example was added by the sender’s provider and proves nothing to the recipient.








Result
Identity checked
Value here




spf=pass
smtp.mailfrom, the envelope domain
mailer.esp.example


dkim=pass
header.d, the signing domain, with header.s the selector
example.org, selector esp2026


dmarc=pass
header.from, the author domain
example.org



SPF passed for the provider’s domain, which does not align with example.org. DMARC still passes, because DKIM passed and its d= matches the From domain.


Which headers can be trusted?
Only those added by systems you control: everything at and above your own boundary MX’s first Received header. Anything below it was written by the sender or by servers you do not operate, and can be forged, including Received and Authentication-Results headers. A well-behaved receiver removes Authentication-Results headers that claim its own authserv-id before adding its own.
Forwarding and mailing lists break SPF (a new IP) and often DKIM (a modified subject or footer). ARC (RFC 8617, Experimental) lets intermediaries record the results they saw; receivers decide whether to trust a given intermediary.


Pulling headers apart in PowerShell
Header lines are folded: a line beginning with a space or tab continues the previous header. Unfold first, then parse:
function Get-MailHeader {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Splits the headers of a saved message (.eml) into one object per header, in the order they appear.
    .EXAMPLE
        Get-MailHeader -Path .\constructed-headers.eml | Where-Object Name -eq 'Received'
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string]$Path
    )

    $Raw = Get-Content -LiteralPath $Path -Raw

    # The headers end at the first blank line
    $HeaderBlock = ($Raw -split "\r?\n\r?\n", 2)[0]

    # A line starting with a space or tab continues the header above it ("folding"); join them back up
    $Unfolded = $HeaderBlock -replace '\r?\n[ \t]+', ' '

    # Order 0 is the top header, which the last server added
    $Order = 0
    $Unfolded -split '\r?\n' |
        ForEach-Object {
            $Name, $Value = $_ -split ':\s*', 2
            [pscustomobject]@{ Order = $Order++; Name = $Name; Value = $Value }
        }
}
# Path, oldest hop first
Get-MailHeader -Path .\constructed-headers.eml |
    Where-Object Name -eq 'Received' |
    Sort-Object Order -Descending |
    Format-Table Order, Value -Wrap

Get-MailHeader -Path .\constructed-headers.eml |
    Where-Object Name -in 'Return-Path', 'From', 'Reply-To', 'Authentication-Results'

title: Email security
text:
SPF
What SPF checks: is the connecting IP allowed to send mail for the envelope domain? RFC 7208 evaluates the MAIL FROM domain, or the HELO/EHLO name when MAIL FROM is empty (bounces). It never looks at the From header.
example.org.  TXT  "v=spf1 ip4:192.0.2.0/24 include:_spf.esp.example -all"



Mechanism
Matches when the IP…




ip4:, ip6:
is in the address or range


a, mx
is an A/AAAA address of the domain, or of its MX hosts


include:
passes the SPF policy of another domain


exists:
makes a constructed name resolve (advanced)


all
always; used last


ptr
reverse DNS matches; “SHOULD NOT” be used



Each mechanism takes a qualifier: + pass (default), - fail, ~ softfail, ? neutral. Results are pass, fail, softfail, neutral, none, temperror and permerror.
Limits that cause real outages: at most 10 mechanisms and modifiers that need DNS lookups (include, a, mx, ptr, exists, redirect) per evaluation, counting nested includes, and at most 2 lookups that return nothing (RFC 7208 §4.6.4). Exceeding them is a permerror, which DMARC treats as not passing. Only one SPF record per name is allowed; two is also a permerror.
SPF pass does not necessarily mean DMARC pass. It passes for the envelope domain. If that is a provider’s bounce domain, SPF is not aligned with the From domain.

title: Email security
text:
DKIM
What DKIM signs and verifies: a signature over chosen header fields and the body, made with the signing domain’s private key. The receiver fetches the public key from DNS and verifies. RFC 6376.
DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; c=relaxed/relaxed; d=example.org;
    s=esp2026; t=1792177329; h=from:to:subject:date:message-id;
    bh=47DEQpj8HBSa+/TImW+5JCeuQeRkm5NMpJWZG3hSuFU=; b=Qx3fK9aL...

esp2026._domainkey.example.org.  TXT  "v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkqh..."







Tag
Meaning




d=
Signing domain: the identity DKIM authenticates, and what DMARC compares


s=
Selector: the key is at <s>._domainkey.<d>


a=
Algorithm, rsa-sha256 or ed25519-sha256


h=
Header fields covered; from is required


bh=
Hash of the canonicalized body


b=
The signature


c=
Canonicalization for header/body, simple or relaxed: how tolerant it is of whitespace changes


t=, x=
Signature time and optional expiry


l=
Body length signed; anything after it is unsigned, so avoid it



The d= domain does not have to match the From domain; DKIM only says “this domain took responsibility for this message.” DMARC is what requires a match. An empty p= in the key record means the key was revoked.

title: Email security
text:
DMARC
DMARC (RFC 9989, May 2026) ties SPF and DKIM to the domain the user sees.

Start with the domain in the message From header. Look up _dmarc.<that domain>, walking up toward the organizational domain if there is no record.
A message passes DMARC if SPF or DKIM passes and is aligned with that domain. One is enough.
Alignment. Strict (s): the domains are identical. Relaxed (r, the default): they share an organizational domain, so mail.example.org aligns with example.org.
Policy and reporting. If DMARC fails, the domain owner’s policy asks receivers to do nothing (none), treat it as suspicious (quarantine) or reject it, and where to send reports.

_dmarc.example.org.  TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@example.org"

DMARC tags (RFC 9989 §4.7)









Tag
Meaning
Values
Default

DMARC1
required


p
Policy for the domain
none, quarantine, reject
none if absent


sp
Policy for existing subdomains
as p
p

Policy for non-existent subdomains
as p
sp, then p

DKIM alignment
r, s
r


aspf
SPF alignment
r, s
r


t
Test mode: asks receivers not to apply the policy
y, n
n

Aggregate report destinations
URIs
none


ruf
Failure report destinations
URIs
none


fo
Which failures generate failure reports
0, 1, d, s
0


psd
Whether this is a public suffix domain
y, n, u
u





Alignment checker
Pick a worked example, or enter the identities from your own message. Work out the result, then select Show answer. The organizational domain is filled in as the last two labels of the From domain; that is an approximation. Real receivers find it with the DNS tree walk in RFC 9989 §4.10, so correct it for names like example.k12.wi.us.


Load example

learndmarc example 1
learndmarc example 2
learndmarc example 3

MAIL FROM domain (RFC5321.MailFrom)

passfailsoftfailneutralnonetemperrorpermerror

Show answer







Work through email headers
These three exercises are from learndmarc.com, which builds and sends a test message and shows each step. Transcripts are reproduced as text. For each one, identify the sender identities, the SPF and DKIM results, and whether the message passes DMARC, and why.

Example 1
. 220 smtp.learndmarc.com ESMTP Postfix
> HELO red.secondary.com
. 250 smtp.learndmarc.com Hello red.secondary.com <153.112.107.49>
> MAIL FROM: <gina@red.secondary.com>
. 250 Ok
> RCPT TO: <someone@yahoo.com>
> DATA
> From: "Gina" <gina@blue.secondary.com>
> DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; d=primary.com; s=selector; (DKIM Auth Result: PASS)
> Subject: Who reads the subject anyway?

Policies:
DMARC policy _dmarc.blue.secondary.com: "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; t=y;"
SPF policy red.secondary.com: "v=spf1 ip4:182.107.92.190 -all"
SPF policy blue.secondary.com: "v=spf1 ip4:24.121.50.128 ~all"


Answer

DMARC fails, the message will NOT be treated as suspicious.

Domain part red.secondary.com from the RFC5321.MailFrom address (MAIL FROM:) is used to retrieve the SPF policy.
Domain part blue.secondary.com from the RFC5322.From address (From:) is used to check DMARC alignment.
The message is signed with a DKIM signature and passed validation.
SPF failed because source IP address 153.112.107.49 is NOT allowed to send on behalf of red.secondary.com.
Having t=y in a DMARC policy signals that the Domain Owner is in test mode and requests that mail receivers not apply the stated handling policies (p, sp, or np) to messages that fail validation checks.
The DMARC alignment policy is ‘relaxed’. This is because the ‘aspf’ and ‘adkim’ elements were not specified or had an ‘r’ value. This means that only the organizational domains have to be in alignment.
DKIM passed validation but there is NO alignment (primary.com != secondary.com).
DMARC failed because neither SPF or DKIM passed validation and have alignment.

Note: had SPF passed, red.secondary.com would have aligned with blue.secondary.com under relaxed alignment: both have the organizational domain secondary.com.



Example 2
. 220 smtp.learndmarc.com ESMTP Postfix
> HELO red.primary.com
. 250 smtp.learndmarc.com Hello red.primary.com <97.196.174.88>
> MAIL FROM: <terry@red.primary.com>
. 250 Ok
> RCPT TO: <someone@hotmail.com>
> DATA
> From: "Terry" <terry@blue.primary.com>
> DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; d=secondary.com; s=selector; (DKIM Auth Result: FAIL)
> Subject: I'll let myself out

Policies:
DMARC policy _dmarc.blue.primary.com: "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; adkim=s; aspf=s;"
SPF policy red.primary.com: "v=spf1 ip4:95.129.128.101 ~all"
SPF policy blue.primary.com: "v=spf1 ip4:44.62.173.139 ~all"


Answer

DMARC fails, the message will be quarantined.

Domain part red.primary.com from the RFC5321.MailFrom address (MAIL FROM:) is used to retrieve the SPF policy.
Domain part blue.primary.com from the RFC5322.From address (From:) is used to check DMARC alignment.
The message is signed with a DKIM signature but failed validation (auth result ‘fail’), the message has been altered.
SPF failed because source IP address 97.196.174.88 is NOT allowed to send on behalf of red.primary.com.
The DMARC alignment policy is ‘strict’. The ‘aspf’ and ‘adkim’ elements have an ‘s’ value. This means that both domain and subdomain need to be an exact match.
DMARC failed because neither SPF or DKIM passed validation and have alignment.
DMARC failed and the policy is set to ‘quarantine’ so the requested action is to quarantine the message.

Note: the SPF record ends in ~all, so learndmarc’s “failed” is strictly an SPF softfail. For DMARC the distinction does not matter: only pass counts.



Example 3
. 220 smtp.learndmarc.com ESMTP Postfix
> HELO blue.secondary.com
. 250 smtp.learndmarc.com Hello blue.secondary.com <156.157.23.197>
> MAIL FROM: <ray@blue.secondary.com>
. 250 Ok
> RCPT TO: <someone@gmail.com>
> DATA
> From: "Ray" <ray@red.primary.com>
> DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; d=blue.primary.com; s=selector; (DKIM Auth Result: PASS)
> Subject: DMARC test

Policies:
DMARC policy _dmarc.red.primary.com: "v=DMARC1; p=none; adkim=s; aspf=s;"
SPF policy blue.secondary.com: "v=spf1 ip4:62.165.120.61 ~all"
SPF policy red.primary.com: "v=spf1 ip4:156.157.23.197 -all"


Answer

DMARC fails, the message will NOT be treated as suspicious.

Domain part blue.secondary.com from the RFC5321.MailFrom address (MAIL FROM:) is used to retrieve the SPF policy.
Domain part red.primary.com from the RFC5322.From address (From:) is used to check DMARC alignment.
The message is signed with a DKIM signature and passed validation.
SPF failed because source IP address 156.157.23.197 is NOT allowed to send on behalf of blue.secondary.com.
The DMARC alignment policy is ‘strict’. The ‘aspf’ and ‘adkim’ elements have an ‘s’ value. This means that both domain and subdomain need to be an exact match.
DKIM passed validation but there is NO alignment (blue.primary.com != red.primary.com).
DMARC failed because neither SPF or DKIM passed validation and have alignment.
DMARC failed but the policy is set to ‘none’ so no action will be taken.

Notes: the sending IP is listed in red.primary.com’s SPF record, which is a trap: SPF is evaluated for the MAIL FROM domain, not the From domain. And under relaxed alignment, the DKIM signature from blue.primary.com would have aligned with red.primary.com.

The answers above are learndmarc’s explanations; the notes are additions.

Common problems:







Symptom
Likely cause




SPF permerror
Two SPF records, a syntax error, or more than 10 DNS-lookup mechanisms after nested includes


SPF passes, DMARC fails
The envelope domain is the provider’s, so SPF is not aligned; set up DKIM with your domain as d=, or a custom return-path domain


DKIM fail for one sender only
Wrong selector published, key rotated without DNS update, or a gateway that modifies messages after signing


DKIM passes, DMARC fails
The provider signs with its own domain; configure signing with your domain


Legitimate mail quarantined after moving to p=quarantine
A sender that was never inventoried; the aggregate reports would have shown it


Forwarded mail fails
Forwarding breaks SPF; DKIM survives only if the forwarder does not modify the message



Look up the DKIM selector from a real message’s DKIM-Signature (s=), not by guessing.

title: Email security
text:
DMARC reporting and the 2026 RFCs

Aggregate reports (RFC 9990)
Receivers send daily-ish XML summaries to the rua address: for each sending IP, how many messages, the SPF and DKIM results, whether each aligned, and the disposition applied. RFC 9990 defines the format. Reports are usually gzip-compressed attachments. This is how you find every service sending as your domain before you move from p=none to enforcement.
Sending reports to another domain (a vendor or a CRT-run mailbox) requires the destination to agree. For _dmarc.example.org with rua=mailto:reports@dmarc.vendor.example, receivers check for:
example.org._report._dmarc.dmarc.vendor.example.  TXT  "v=DMARC1"
Without it they ignore that rua URI. This stops a domain from flooding a victim with reports.


Failure reports (RFC 9991)
Per-message reports to the ruf address, controlled by fo. RFC 9991 warns they can contain full headers and content, including personal information; many large receivers do not send them. Aggregate reports are the recommended default.


What changed from RFC 7489
RFC 9989 obsoletes RFC 7489 and RFC 9091 and moves DMARC to the Standards Track (Appendix C):







Change
Detail




pct removed
Partial enforcement by percentage is gone; t=y replaces part of its function


t added
Test mode: request that receivers not apply the policy


np added
Policy for non-existent subdomains (from RFC 9091)


psd added
Flags public suffix domains


rf, ri removed
Report format and interval tags


Organizational domain
Found by a DNS tree walk of _dmarc records (at most 8 queries) instead of the Public Suffix List


Reporting split out
Aggregate reporting is RFC 9990, failure reporting RFC 9991


Terminology
“Domain Owner Assessment Policy,” “Enforcement,” “Monitoring Mode”; “Report Receiver” became “Report Consumer”



Existing v=DMARC1 records keep working; unknown tags are ignored, so a leftover pct= does no harm but no longer does anything for receivers that follow RFC 9989.

title: Email security
text:
Other email security mechanisms

MTA-STS and TLS reporting
SMTP between servers uses opportunistic STARTTLS: an attacker on the path can strip it, and senders do not validate certificates by default. MTA-STS (RFC 8461) lets a domain publish that its MX hosts support TLS with valid certificates, and that senders should refuse to deliver otherwise.
_mta-sts.example.org.  TXT  "v=STSv1; id=20261016T000000;"
The policy is served over HTTPS at https://mta-sts.example.org/.well-known/mta-sts.txt:
version: STSv1
mode: enforce
mx: mail.example.org
max_age: 604800
Start with mode: testing, and change id whenever the policy changes so senders refetch it.
TLS-RPT (RFC 8460) asks senders to report TLS negotiation failures, which is how you find out MTA-STS (or an expired MX certificate) is blocking mail:
_smtp._tls.example.org.  TXT  "v=TLSRPTv1; rua=mailto:tlsrpt@example.org"


Sender ID (historical)
Microsoft’s Sender ID (RFC 4406) checked a “purported responsible address” taken from the message headers rather than the envelope, and reused v=spf2.0 records. The IETF experiment was concluded in RFC 6686 (2012), which found SPF in wide use and Sender ID not. If you find spf2.0/pra records, they are leftovers.

title: Passwords
text:
Something you know, something you are, something you have.
Passwords are something you know; we refer to them as secrets. Other types of secrets: passphrases, PINs, secret questions.
The goal in all authentication methods is good enough uniqueness.
We can add behavior to assist in making risk assessments.

NIST SP 800-63B-4 uses the same three factors: something you know (a password or PIN), something you have (a cryptographic device or authenticator app), and something you are (a biometric, which NIST only permits in combination with something you have). Behavior (where a sign-in comes from, what device, at what time) is not an authentication factor on its own, but it feeds the risk decisions around authentication: whether to ask for another factor, block or alert.

title: Passwords
text:
Entropy

“My greatest concern was what to call it. I thought of calling it ‘information,’ but the word was overly used, so I decided to call it ‘uncertainty.’ When I discussed it with John von Neumann, he had a better idea. Von Neumann told me, ‘You should call it entropy, for two reasons. In the first place your uncertainty function has been used in statistical mechanics under that name, so it already has a name. In the second place, and more important, no one really knows what entropy really is, so in a debate you will always have the advantage.’”
— Claude Shannon, as recounted in M. Tribus and E. C. McIrvine, “Energy and Information,” Scientific American 225(3), 1971


The model

Bits of entropy (aka shannons) = log2(search space)
Search space = alphabetlength

So each character adds log2(alphabet) bits:



Alphabet

Multiplicative versus exponential. Length is the exponent. Making the alphabet bigger multiplies the search space once per character; making the password longer multiplies the whole search space by the alphabet size again. Going from 26 to 95 characters adds under 2 bits per character. Going from 8 to 15 lowercase characters adds 33 bits.
The assumption that matters. The formula is only true when every character (or word) is chosen uniformly at random. Human-chosen passwords are not: Summer2026! uses a 95-character alphabet at length 11 and the formula says 72 bits, but it is a capitalized dictionary word, a year and a symbol: exactly the pattern a wordlist with rules tries first. Treat the calculator as an upper bound for random secrets, such as those a password manager generates.


Entropy in PowerShell
Bits of entropy for a random password, from the alphabet size and length:
function Get-PasswordEntropy {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Bits of entropy for a password chosen at random.
    .EXAMPLE
        Get-PasswordEntropy -AlphabetSize 95 -Length 8
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        # How many symbols each character is picked from: 10 for digits, 26 for lowercase, 95 for printable ASCII
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [ValidateRange(2, [int]::MaxValue)]
        [int]$AlphabetSize,

        # How many characters (or words) are in the password
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [ValidateRange(1, [int]::MaxValue)]
        [int]$Length
    )

    # Bits = log2(alphabet ^ length), which is the same as length x log2(alphabet)
    $Bits = $Length * [math]::Log($AlphabetSize, 2)
    [math]::Round($Bits, 1)
}
And the reverse: how long a password from a given alphabet must be to match a number of bits. Round up, because a partial character is not possible.
function Get-PasswordLengthForEntropy {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
        How long a random password must be to reach a number of bits of entropy.
    .EXAMPLE
        Get-PasswordLengthForEntropy -AlphabetSize 26 -Bits 52.6
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        # How many symbols each character is picked from
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [ValidateRange(2, [int]::MaxValue)]
        [int]$AlphabetSize,

        # The entropy to match, in bits
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [ValidateRange(1, 1024)]
        [double]$Bits
    )

    # Each character adds log2(alphabet) bits
    $BitsPerCharacter = [math]::Log($AlphabetSize, 2)

    # Round away tiny floating-point error, then round up: a partial character is not possible
    [math]::Ceiling([math]::Round($Bits / $BitsPerCharacter, 6))
}
Get-PasswordEntropy -AlphabetSize 95 -Length 8               # 52.6
Get-PasswordLengthForEntropy -AlphabetSize 26 -Bits 52.6     # 12 lowercase letters match 8 printable ASCII characters
Get-PasswordLengthForEntropy -AlphabetSize 7776 -Bits 128    # 10 EFF words reach 128 bits

text:
Cracking = time x money

Who is the threat?
How is it protected?

An offline attacker who has the hashes guesses as fast as their hardware allows; nothing on your side slows them down except the hashing algorithm. So the two questions are: how much hardware can this attacker bring, and how expensive did we make each guess?
Money buys time, not guesses. Searching a given space takes a fixed number of GPU-hours. Ten times the GPUs finishes ten times sooner for the same energy bill, but needs ten times the power and cooling while it runs. The cost below excludes the purchase price of the equipment, as an attacker who already owns it would see it.

Cracking time and cost explorer
Uses the alphabet and length from the calculator above. Each cell shows the time to search the entire space for one hash, and the cost of that effort. Every GPU leaves as heat the power it draws, so the second table shows the cooling each tier needs. Dollar figures, GPU counts and wattage are editable assumptions, not measurements.

A stored NT hash and an NTLM protocol exchange are different things. The NT hash is what sits in the domain database; an attacker gets it by stealing NTDS.dit, a backup, or replication rights. NetNTLMv2 is a challenge-response captured from the network or a coerced authentication. Both lead to the password, at very different speeds, and the NT hash can be used directly without cracking it (pass-the-hash). See Microsoft’s Passwords technical overview.

title: Passwords
text:
Protecting users

Do what we can to protect users.
Attack modeling should be based on online attacks.
We have duties to protect hashes from getting stolen.

Online attacks are the ones we control. NIST SP 800-63B-4 §3.2.2 requires verifiers to limit consecutive failed attempts on an account to no more than 100. Against a throttled login, an attacker gets a handful of guesses per account, so the question is not “how many bits” but “is this password on the list of the first hundred things anyone tries.” That is why the blocklist matters more than the entropy figure. Spraying one common password across many accounts stays under per-account limits, which is another reason the blocklist and MFA matter.
Offline attacks happen after we failed to protect the hashes. Once hashes are stolen, only the hashing scheme stands between the attacker and the passwords. NIST §3.1.1.2 requires passwords be salted (at least 32 bits) and hashed with a suitable password hashing scheme, with the cost factor “as high as practical without negatively impacting verifier performance.” OWASP’s current minimums:







Scheme
OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet minimum




Argon2id
19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, parallelism 1


scrypt
N = 217 (128 MiB), r = 8, p = 1


bcrypt
Work factor 10 or more; legacy use; 72-byte input limit in most implementations


PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256
600,000 iterations



Windows does not give you that choice for domain accounts: the NT hash is unsalted and fast. Protecting it means protecting where it lives: domain controllers, their backups, and the accounts and rights that can replicate directory secrets.

Check a password against Pwned Passwords
Have I Been Pwned’s Pwned Passwords range API uses k-anonymity: you send the first five characters of the password’s SHA-1 hash and compare the returned suffixes locally. The password and the full hash never leave your machine.
function Test-PwnedPassword {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Checks a password against Have I Been Pwned's Pwned Passwords, without sending the password.
    .EXAMPLE
        Test-PwnedPassword -Password (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'Password')
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        # A SecureString, so the password is not shown on screen or saved in history
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [securestring]$Password
    )

    # Turn the SecureString back into text, then into bytes, and hash it with SHA-1
    $Plain = [System.Net.NetworkCredential]::new('', $Password).Password
    $Bytes = [System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($Plain)
    $HashBytes = [System.Security.Cryptography.SHA1]::Create().ComputeHash($Bytes)
    $Hash = -join ($HashBytes | ForEach-Object { $_.ToString('X2') })

    # Only the first five characters of the hash leave this machine
    $Prefix = $Hash.Substring(0, 5)
    $Suffix = $Hash.Substring(5)
    Write-Verbose "Sending only the prefix $Prefix"
    $Response = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/$Prefix"

    # The reply is one "SUFFIX:COUNT" per line; look for ours locally
    $Match = $Response -split "`r?`n" | Where-Object { $_.StartsWith("${Suffix}:") }
    [pscustomobject]@{
        Pwned = [bool]$Match
        Count = if ($Match) { [int]($Match -split ':')[1] } else { 0 }
    }
}
Test-PwnedPassword -Password (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'Password') -Verbose
P@ssw0rd returns Pwned: True with a count in the millions.
