title: PowerShell
text:
Administration, automation, and analysis.
Turning a repetitive task into something repeatable.

PowerShell commands return objects, not text. A file has a Length and a LastWriteTimeUtc; an event has an Id and a TimeCreated. You filter and sort on those properties directly instead of cutting columns out of text, and the result is the same whether the output is 10 lines or 10 million.
Everything on this page runs in Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7 unless noted.

title: PowerShell
text:
Administration, automation, and analysis.
Turning a repetitive task into something repeatable.

PowerShell commands return objects, not text. A file has a Length and a LastWriteTimeUtc; an event has an Id and a TimeCreated. You filter and sort on those properties directly instead of cutting columns out of text, and the result is the same whether the output is 10 lines or 10 million.
Everything on this page runs in Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7 unless noted.

title: PowerShell
text:
Finding commands
Get-Command finds commands; Get-Help explains them. Commands are named Verb-Noun, so search by either half.
Get-Command -Noun WinEvent                       # everything that works on event logs
Get-Command -Verb Export                         # every way to write something out
Get-Command *hash*                               # wildcards work too
Get-Help Get-WinEvent -Examples
Get-Help Get-WinEvent -Parameter FilterHashtable
Get-Command Get-FileHash -Syntax                 # parameter sets at a glance
(Get-Command Get-FileHash).OutputType            # what it returns
Local help is minimal until you run Update-Help (from an elevated prompt in Windows PowerShell 5.1). Get-Help <command> -Online opens the current Microsoft Learn page instead.

Figure out what a command returns
Pipe it to Get-Member. The first line is the type; the list is what you can select, filter and sort on.
Get-Item C:\Windows\notepad.exe | Get-Member -MemberType Property
   TypeName: System.IO.FileInfo

Name              MemberType Definition
----              ---------- ----------
Attributes        Property   System.IO.FileAttributes Attributes {get;set;}
CreationTime      Property   datetime CreationTime {get;set;}
CreationTimeUtc   Property   datetime CreationTimeUtc {get;set;}
...
Length            Property   long Length {get;}
Name              Property   string Name {get;}

title: PowerShell
text:
Objects and the pipeline
The pipeline passes objects from one command to the next (about_Pipelines). The default table view shows only some properties; Select-Object chooses which, and Format-List * shows all of them.
Get-Item C:\Windows\notepad.exe | Format-List *
Get-Item C:\Windows\notepad.exe | Select-Object Name, Length, LastWriteTime, VersionInfo
A calculated property adds a column computed from each object:
Get-ChildItem -Path .\Case -File |
    Select-Object Name, @{ n = 'SizeMB'; e = { [math]::Round($_.Length / 1MB, 2) } }
Parameters bind from the pipeline by value (the whole object) or by property name. That is why Get-ChildItem | Get-FileHash works: Get-FileHash accepts the file’s path from each object.

title: PowerShell
text:
Working with data







Command
Use




Where-Object
Keep objects that match: Where-Object Length -gt 10MB, Where-Object { $_.Name -like '*.ps1' -and $_.Length -lt 1KB }


Sort-Object
Order by one or more properties: Sort-Object Length -Descending


Group-Object
Count by a property: Group-Object Extension


Measure-Object
Count, sum, minimum, maximum: Measure-Object Length -Sum -Maximum


Select-Object
Choose properties; -First, -Last, -Unique, -ExpandProperty


Export-Csv
Write objects to CSV for Excel or Timeline Explorer


ConvertTo-Json
Write objects to JSON


Out-GridView
Interactive, filterable window (Windows only)



Get-ChildItem -Path .\Case -Recurse -File |
    Where-Object Length -gt 10MB |
    Sort-Object Length -Descending |
    Select-Object FullName, Length, LastWriteTimeUtc |
    Export-Csv .\LargeFiles.csv -NoTypeInformation
Filter as far left as you can. Get-ChildItem -Filter *.evtx and Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable filter at the source; Where-Object sees every object first.

title: PowerShell
text:
Example tasks

Working with an existing collection of files
# What is here, by type
Get-ChildItem -Path .\Case -Recurse -File |
    Group-Object Extension |
    Sort-Object Count -Descending |
    Select-Object Count, Name

# Hash everything
Get-ChildItem -Path .\Case -Recurse -File |
    Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 |
    Select-Object Hash, Path |
    Export-Csv .\Hashes.csv -NoTypeInformation

# Files modified in a window (UTC)
$Start = [datetime]'2026-10-01T00:00:00Z'
$End = [datetime]'2026-10-08T00:00:00Z'
Get-ChildItem -Path .\Case -Recurse -File |
    Where-Object { $_.LastWriteTimeUtc -ge $Start.ToUniversalTime() -and $_.LastWriteTimeUtc -lt $End.ToUniversalTime() } |
    Sort-Object LastWriteTimeUtc
Once you have typed the same pipeline twice, make it a function. Get-FileInventory combines the listing and the hashing into one object per file:
function Get-FileInventory {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Lists every file under a folder with its size, UTC timestamps and hash.
    .DESCRIPTION
        For a collection of files you were given. Reading a file can update its last access
        time on the analysis machine, so work on a copy.
    .EXAMPLE
        Get-FileInventory -Path D:\Case\Collected | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 10
    .EXAMPLE
        Get-FileInventory -Path D:\Case\Collected | Export-Csv D:\Case\Output\Inventory.csv -NoTypeInformation
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        # The folder to inventory
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [ValidateScript({ Test-Path -Path $_ -PathType Container })]
        [string]$Path,

        # Any algorithm Get-FileHash supports
        [ValidateSet('MD5', 'SHA1', 'SHA256', 'SHA512')]
        [string]$Algorithm = 'SHA256'
    )

    # The folder's full path, so each file can be shown relative to it
    $Root = (Resolve-Path -Path $Path).ProviderPath.TrimEnd('\')

    # -Force includes hidden and system files
    Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $Root -Recurse -File -Force |
        ForEach-Object {
            $Hash = Get-FileHash -LiteralPath $_.FullName -Algorithm $Algorithm
            [pscustomobject]@{
                RelativePath     = $_.FullName.Substring($Root.Length + 1)
                Extension        = $_.Extension.ToLower()
                Length           = $_.Length
                CreationTimeUtc  = $_.CreationTimeUtc
                LastWriteTimeUtc = $_.LastWriteTimeUtc
                Hash             = $Hash.Hash
            }
        }
}
Get-FileInventory -Path D:\Case\Collected |
    Sort-Object Length -Descending |
    Select-Object -First 10

Get-FileInventory -Path D:\Case\Collected |
    Export-Csv D:\Case\Output\Inventory.csv -NoTypeInformation
The function returns objects and leaves the CSV to Export-Csv. That keeps it small, and the same output can go to the screen, a CSV or the next command.


Looking at collected Windows event logs with Get-WinEvent
Query the copied .evtx file with -Path, not the live log on the analysis machine (Get-WinEvent).
# What providers and IDs are in this log, and how many
Get-WinEvent -Path .\Case\Logs\System.evtx |
    Group-Object ProviderName, Id |
    Sort-Object Count -Descending |
    Select-Object -First 15 Count, Name

# Logons and failed logons, filtered at the source
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    Path = '.\Case\Logs\Security.evtx'
    Id = 4624, 4625
    StartTime = [datetime]'2026-10-01'
} |
    Group-Object Id |
    Select-Object Count, Name
Get-EvtxSummary turns the first example into a function, with the first and last time each event appears:
function Get-EvtxSummary {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Counts the events in a collected .evtx file by provider and event ID, with the first and last time each appears.
    .EXAMPLE
        Get-EvtxSummary -Path .\Case\Logs\System.evtx | Format-Table
    .EXAMPLE
        Get-ChildItem .\Case\Logs -Filter *.evtx | Get-EvtxSummary -Id 4624, 4625, 7045
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        # A saved .evtx file; also accepts files piped from Get-ChildItem
        [Parameter(Mandatory, ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName)]
        [Alias('FullName')]
        [string]$Path,

        # Only count these event IDs
        [int[]]$Id
    )

    process {
        # Path reads the saved file instead of the live log on this machine
        $Filter = @{ Path = (Resolve-Path -Path $Path).ProviderPath }
        if ($Id) {
            $Filter.Id = $Id
        }

        # Get-WinEvent reports "no events found" as an error; SilentlyContinue turns that into no output
        Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable $Filter -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
            Group-Object ProviderName, Id |
            ForEach-Object {
                $Times = $_.Group.TimeCreated | Sort-Object
                [pscustomobject]@{
                    File         = Split-Path -Path $Path -Leaf
                    ProviderName = $_.Group[0].ProviderName
                    Id           = $_.Group[0].Id
                    Count        = $_.Count
                    First        = $Times[0]
                    Last         = $Times[-1]
                }
            } |
            Sort-Object Count -Descending
    }
}
Get-EvtxSummary -Path D:\Case\Collected\Logs\System.evtx | Format-Table

# Service installs (7045) in every log under the case
Get-ChildItem D:\Case\Collected -Filter *.evtx -Recurse | Get-EvtxSummary -Id 7045
File        ProviderName              Id Count First                 Last
----        ------------              -- ----- -----                 ----
System.evtx Service Control Manager 7045     4 10/16/2026 9:27:25 PM 10/16/2026 11:09:27 PM
Event properties hold the event’s data fields. To get named fields, such as TargetUserName and IpAddress in a 4624, read the event XML. Get-LogonEvent does that for successful logons:
function Get-LogonEvent {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Successful logons (event 4624) from a collected Security.evtx, with the user, logon type and source address.
    .EXAMPLE
        Get-LogonEvent -Path .\Case\Logs\Security.evtx | Group-Object LogonType
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        # A saved Security.evtx
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string]$Path,

        # Stop after this many events, newest first; a Security log can hold millions
        [int]$MaxEvents = 1000
    )

    $Filter = @{ Path = (Resolve-Path -Path $Path).ProviderPath; Id = 4624 }
    Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable $Filter -MaxEvents $MaxEvents |
        ForEach-Object {
            # The named fields (TargetUserName, LogonType, IpAddress...) are in the event's XML
            $Data = @{}
            ([xml]$_.ToXml()).Event.EventData.Data | ForEach-Object { $Data[$_.Name] = $_.'#text' }

            [pscustomobject]@{
                TimeCreated = $_.TimeCreated
                User        = '{0}\{1}' -f $Data.TargetDomainName, $Data.TargetUserName
                LogonType   = $Data.LogonType
                IpAddress   = $Data.IpAddress
            }
        }
}
Get-LogonEvent -Path D:\Case\Collected\Logs\Security.evtx |
    Group-Object LogonType |
    Select-Object Count, Name

title: PowerShell
text:
Making a script reusable

Parameters instead of hard-coded values.
Functions, -Verbose, -WhatIf where applicable.
An example of automating part of the DFIR box build: New-CaseFolder, below, creates the folders for each case.


Parameters
[CmdletBinding()]
param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory)]
    [ValidateScript({ Test-Path -Path $_ -PathType Container })]
    [string]$Path,

    [ValidateSet('SHA1', 'SHA256', 'SHA512')]
    [string]$Algorithm = 'SHA256',

    [switch]$IncludeHidden
)
[CmdletBinding()] makes a script or function an advanced function: it gets -Verbose, -Debug, -ErrorAction and the other common parameters for free. Validation attributes reject bad input before your code runs. A comment on the line above a parameter becomes its help text in Get-Help.


-WhatIf, -Confirm and ShouldProcess
Anything that changes state should support -WhatIf. Declare SupportsShouldProcess and wrap each change in $PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess() (about_Functions_CmdletBindingAttribute):
function New-CaseFolder {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Creates the Collected, Output and Notes folders for a case. Supports -WhatIf.
    .EXAMPLE
        New-CaseFolder -CaseRoot E:\Cases -CaseNumber 2026-0142 -WhatIf
    #>
    [CmdletBinding(SupportsShouldProcess)]
    param(
        # Where case folders live, such as a persistent disk or share
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string]$CaseRoot,

        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string]$CaseNumber
    )

    $CasePath = Join-Path -Path $CaseRoot -ChildPath $CaseNumber
    'Collected', 'Output', 'Notes' |
        ForEach-Object { Join-Path -Path $CasePath -ChildPath $_ } |
        Where-Object { -not (Test-Path -Path $_) } |
        ForEach-Object {
            # ShouldProcess returns $false under -WhatIf, and prints what would have happened
            if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($_, 'Create folder')) {
                New-Item -Path $_ -ItemType Directory | Out-Null
                Write-Verbose "Created $_"
            }
        }
}
New-CaseFolder -CaseRoot E:\Cases -CaseNumber 2026-0142 -WhatIf
What if: Performing the operation "Create folder" on target "E:\Cases\2026-0142\Collected".
What if: Performing the operation "Create folder" on target "E:\Cases\2026-0142\Output".
What if: Performing the operation "Create folder" on target "E:\Cases\2026-0142\Notes".
Commands you call inside inherit -WhatIf, so New-Item inside a function run with -WhatIf would not create anything either; the explicit ShouldProcess call gives a clear message and covers non-cmdlet work such as winget or registry edits.


Error handling
PowerShell has non-terminating errors (the command reports and keeps going: one unreadable file in a recursive listing) and terminating errors (the command stops). try/catch only catches terminating errors, so add -ErrorAction Stop where you want to handle a failure:
try {
    $Events = Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable $Filter -ErrorAction Stop
}
catch {
    if ($_.FullyQualifiedErrorId -like 'NoMatchingEventsFound*') {
        $Events = @()
    }
    else {
        throw
    }
}
Get-WinEvent reports “No events were found that match the specified selection criteria” as an error. Get-EvtxSummary uses -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue instead, which is simpler but also hides other problems, such as a damaged file. To collect non-terminating errors without stopping, add -ErrorVariable Problems and look at $Problems afterward.


Building collections
Let the pipeline build arrays. $Results = foreach (...) { [pscustomobject]@{...} } and $Results = ... | ForEach-Object { ... } collect output efficiently; appending with $Results += $Item copies the whole array on every addition and gets slow with large data. When you do need to add items one by one, use [System.Collections.Generic.List[object]]::new() and .Add().

title: PowerShell
text:
Your own module
A function you paste into a window is gone when the window closes. A module keeps your functions in one file that PowerShell loads for you: type the function name in any new window and it works.
A script module is a .psm1 file inside a folder with the same name, in one of the folders listed in $env:PSModulePath (about_Modules). Your personal folder is under Documents:




Personal module folder




PowerShell 7
Documents\PowerShell\Modules


Windows PowerShell 5.1
Documents\WindowsPowerShell\Modules




1. Create the module
# Your Documents folder (it may have been moved to OneDrive)
$Documents = [Environment]::GetFolderPath('MyDocuments')

# For Windows PowerShell 5.1, use 'WindowsPowerShell\Modules\MyTools' instead
$ModuleFolder = Join-Path -Path $Documents -ChildPath 'PowerShell\Modules\MyTools'
New-Item -Path $ModuleFolder -ItemType Directory -Force

# The .psm1 file must have the same name as its folder
$ModuleFile = Join-Path -Path $ModuleFolder -ChildPath 'MyTools.psm1'
New-Item -Path $ModuleFile -ItemType File
notepad $ModuleFile


2. Add functions
Every function on this site is in a code block of its own, separate from the examples that use it. Use the copy button at the top right of the block, paste it into MyTools.psm1, and save. Add as many as you like, one after another.


3. Use it
Import-Module MyTools -Force       # load it now; run again after each edit
Get-Command -Module MyTools        # what it contains
Get-Help Get-PasswordEntropy       # the help block at the top of each function
In a new window you do not need Import-Module: PowerShell loads the module the first time you use one of its functions.
If you see “running scripts is disabled on this system”, Windows PowerShell 5.1 is using the default Restricted execution policy. Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned allows your own files to run, and still blocks unsigned scripts downloaded from the internet.
